**Is mirroring really label-preserving here?** Mostly, but think about it. In nearly every person, the heart sits on the left, so a mirrored chest X-ray shows an anatomy that almost no real patient has. For pneumonia-versus-normal, that doesn't change the answer, and flips are common in published chest X-ray work. For a task that depends on side (where is the heart? which lung is affected?), a flip would silently corrupt the labels. Choosing augmentations is a domain decision. Augmentation is also for **training only**: you evaluate on the X-rays exactly as they arrived.

**Why triage cares more about sensitivity.** The two kinds of mistake cost very different things. A false positive moves a healthy child's X-ray up the queue; a radiologist reads it a little sooner, sees nothing, and moves on, which costs a minute. A false negative leaves a child with pneumonia at the bottom of the queue, maybe for hours. So a triage tool is tuned for **high sensitivity** (catch nearly every case) and accepts lower specificity (some extra reads). The flag-everyone rule has sensitivity 1.0 and specificity 0.0: it never misses, but it also does no triage at all. The interesting question is how much specificity a trained model can keep while holding sensitivity high.

A **Markov decision process (MDP)** formalizes a sequential decision problem as a sequence of   tuples: at each step the agent observes a state, chooses an action, and receives a scalar reward. The Markov assumption says that the next state and reward depend on the current state and action, rather than the full earlier history. The whole trajectory is the elementary unit of evaluation; every reinforcement-learning algorithm ultimately scores agents by some function of the rewards they generate along their trajectories. The simplest such function is just the sum, the *undiscounted return*, which is what you need to compute before anything fancier makes sense.

A **generative adversarial network (GAN)** has a generator that turns random noise into samples and a discriminator that classifies samples as real or generated. The discriminator is just a binary classifier: it sees a batch of real data and a batch of generated data, and it tries to assign label 1 to the real ones and label 0 to the fake ones. Binary cross-entropy on logits gives it a smooth, well-behaved training signal. The harder the discriminator’s job becomes, the more useful its gradient is to the generator on the other side of the game.

A central processing unit (CPU) has a few very fast cores tuned for branchy, serial work; a GPU has thousands of slower cores tuned for the same operation applied to many elements at once. Tiny workloads run faster on a CPU because the GPU’s launch overhead and host–device transfer dominate; large, regular, parallel workloads (matrix multiplies, convolutions, batched elementwise ops) run dramatically faster on a GPU. A useful rough proxy for “should this run on the GPU?” is just how many independent elements the operation touches.

A multi-armed bandit is the simplest possible decision problem: at each step you pick one of a few arms and receive a noisy reward whose distribution depends only on the arm you pulled. The challenge is the *exploration–exploitation tradeoff*: pull the arm that has looked best so far, or try the others in case they’re actually better? Adding attention or replacing both halves with transformer blocks gives the lineage that leads to modern translation systems.

Aggregate accuracy hides what happens at the subgroup level: a model can be 90% accurate overall while being 95% accurate for group A and 70% accurate for group B. A simple fairness diagnostic is to compute the same metric per group and look at the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring groups. A large gap means the model’s quality of service depends on which group you belong to, and calls for investigation of the data, labels, features, and task context before deciding how to address it.

An autoencoder forces information through a *bottleneck* (a hidden representation much smaller than the input) and asks the model to reconstruct the input on the other side. The only way to keep reconstruction error low is to discover an efficient code for the data in the bottleneck. A linear autoencoder with squared-error loss is, in fact, doing principal component analysis in disguise: the optimal bottleneck weights span the top principal directions of the data.

In this module, you build an intrusion detector: something that watches network traffic and raises an alarm when a connection looks like an attack. The data is real. In 1998, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Lincoln Laboratory ran a simulated Air Force network for nine weeks, recorded every connection, and attacked it on a schedule. The KDD Cup 1999 dataset summarizes each connection as one row of 41 features: how long it lasted, which protocol and service it used, how many bytes went each way, how the TCP connection’s setup exchange, or **handshake**, ended ( ; TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol), and a block of "how busy is this host right now" counts over the last two seconds.

In this module, you'll teach a car to drive itself to a destination without crashing, using only what it can see from where it sits. It's the shape of a self-driving or robot-navigation stack at toy scale: perception, a decision, an action, repeat. Nobody hands the car labeled examples of the right move. It learns from **reward**: +1 for arriving, -1 for crashing. That's **reinforcement learning (RL)**, and the technique you'll write, REINFORCE, updates action probabilities using the rewards that followed them. It is an ancestor of methods used to train game agents, robot controllers and chat models.

Knowledge distillation compresses a model by training a small “student” to mimic the outputs of a large “teacher”. The teacher’s outputs are denser supervision than one-hot labels: they encode which classes are *similar*, how confident the teacher is, and which examples are ambiguous. This often lets a much smaller student reach accuracy a same-sized model trained from scratch on hard labels can’t. The teacher stays frozen; only the student trains.

Mean error tells you the average distortion; the worst-case error tells you whether any single weight got mangled badly. In low-bit quantization, the maximum error grows in lockstep with the scale factor, which is set by the largest weight; so a single outlier weight can stretch the scale and degrade the precision available for the rest. Outlier-aware quantization schemes (for example, a separate scale for each channel) exist to keep the worst-case error from blowing up. The simplest diagnostic is just the max absolute difference.

Mode collapse is the classic GAN failure mode: the generator finds one or a few outputs that reliably fool the discriminator and starts producing them no matter what input noise it receives. The samples look fine individually but are nearly identical to each other, and the generator never learns to cover the rest of the data distribution. A cheap diagnostic is the per-feature standard deviation across a batch of samples; when it’s much smaller than the std of real data, you’re likely watching a collapse.

Models are extremely fragile in the face of upstream data changes: a renamed column, a column whose type silently flipped from int to string, or a missing required field can all turn a working pipeline into garbage with no error. Schema tests catch these before they hit the model: assert the field names you expect, the types you expect, and (often) the value ranges you expect, on every batch of incoming data. Tools like Great Expectations, Pandera, and Pydantic exist for the full version of this.

Models trained on one distribution silently degrade when their inputs shift to a different one: seasonal user behavior, new product features, sensor recalibrations. Drift detection compares the distribution of recent inputs to a known reference (often the training data) on each feature. A change in the mean is the bluntest signal; richer detectors compare full histograms or use statistical comparisons of full distributions. Any of them is better than no detector at all, because the failure mode they catch is *silent*.

News sites, protest footage and leaked documents often "anonymize" a face by pixelating it: the face is cut into square blocks and each block is replaced by its average color. It looks unrecognizable to a person. Reinforcement learning agents optimize the reward you give them, which can differ from the behavior you wanted. If there’s an unintended way to score reward (a bug in the simulator, a sensor that’s easier to fool than the world, a side effect that happens to be rewarded), the agent will find it. This is “reward hacking”, and it’s a deeply practical problem: it shows up in everything from game-playing agents that crash the level to recommendation systems that learn to maximize engagement by serving outrage. The first step in catching it is just measuring how often the agent takes the shortcut behavior.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) turns a frozen language model into a knowledge-grounded system by gluing it to an external corpus. At query time, the system encodes the question into a vector, looks up the nearest documents in an embedding index, stuffs them into the prompt as context, and lets the model answer from them. The “retrieve” step is just a nearest-neighbor search in embedding space, and that nearest-neighbor lookup is the piece that determines whether the model has the right facts in front of it at all.

Sampling from a diffusion model is the forward process run in reverse: starting from pure noise, you repeatedly subtract off a little bit of the predicted noise and let some new noise back in. The reverse step needs a mean and a variance; the mean is a closed-form combination of the current sample  , the predicted noise, and the noise-schedule coefficients at this timestep. Computing that mean correctly is the linchpin of denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) sampling. Get the coefficients wrong and the chain drifts away from the data distribution.

Serving one request at a time leaves most of the GPU’s parallelism idle: a single forward pass on a tiny input is bottlenecked by kernel-launch overhead, the cost of starting work on the device; the arithmetic itself is cheap. Batching groups requests together so the GPU does many forward passes in one call, which amortizes the overhead and keeps its compute units busy. The catch is latency (requests have to wait for the batch to fill) so production systems tune the batch size and timeout against the latency budget.

Trained neural networks are typically much larger than they need to be: many weights end up close to zero and contribute almost nothing to the output. Magnitude pruning exploits this by setting every weight whose absolute value is below a threshold to exactly zero; the rest stay untouched. Skipping zero weights during prediction or shrinking their storage requires a representation and computation that exploit those zeros. Pruning is often combined with a brief fine-tuning step to recover any accuracy lost to the zeroed weights.

Training a BPE tokenizer is a loop: count pair frequencies, merge the most common pair into a new symbol, rewrite the sequence using that symbol, repeat. Each merge grows the vocabulary by one and shrinks the sequence, gradually turning common substrings into single tokens. After many iterations, frequent words end up as one token while rare or novel words still decompose into smaller pieces, which is why BPE can represent unseen words made from symbols in its initial vocabulary without an   token.

Training a Q-network on the stream of transitions an agent produces *as it acts* is unstable: consecutive samples are highly correlated, the data distribution shifts as the policy improves, and rare-but-important events get visited only once. A replay buffer fixes all three by storing recent transitions and letting the learner sample random minibatches from the pool. The buffer breaks the temporal correlation, smooths the data distribution, and reuses each transition many times: the standard recipe for sample-efficient deep RL.

Training an RNN means backpropagating gradients *through time* (BPTT): autograd unrolls the recurrence and applies the chain rule across every timestep. Vanishing or exploding gradients in this unrolled graph are the classical motivation for gated cells, which learn how much of a previous state to preserve at each step.

When a new model lands and something looks worse in production, the first job is *triage*: figure out which metrics moved, by how much, and whether the movement is real or noise. The squared-distance objective favors compact clusters.

“Total reward” is the obvious score for a bandit run, but it conflates two things: the unavoidable noise of the environment and the avoidable cost of exploration. *Regret* isolates the second piece by comparing the agent’s reward against the best constant policy, a fixed action-selection rule, in hindsight: pull the arm with the highest expected reward every single step. Sublinear regret means the agent eventually figures out which arm is best; linear regret means it never really does.
